newsitem.title: UK: WTO credibility depends on banana issue-Ecuador.
newsitem.headline: WTO credibility depends on banana issue-Ecuador.

text.p: The credibility of the World Trade Organisation's dispute settlement procedure depends on how the wrangle over EU banana imports is resolved, according to Ecuador, the world's biggest producer.
"Being the main exporters we want to see major changes (in the EU regime)," Teodoro Maldonado, Ecuador's vice minister of foreign trade, told Reuters on Friday.
And he stressed that just like the Caribbean producers the EU system was designed to help, Ecuador was a developing country and was reliant on the trade for much of its export earnings.
Bananas accounted for 28 percent of Ecuadorean export earnings, making them a close second behind oil, he said. There were 1.2 million people dependent on the banana industry.

A WTO appeals board this week examined a submission by the EU on its case for a revision of a dispute panel finding in May that EU banana import regulations violated the body's rules and should be changed.
The results of the appeal are expected in mid-September.

Maldonado was in London to meet British members of parliament, in an effort to put Ecuador's case. He was confident the EU's appeal against the WTO judgement would be rejected and he wanted full compliance from the EU.
Compensation is not a option," he said, adding "what credibility does the WTO have if the EU does not comply?"
Maldonado stressed Ecuador's banana industry was not dominated by foreign companies and refuted the idea that the case was based on protecting US business interests.
"We don't have foreign multinationals owning land," he said.

There were a large number of small producers in Ecuador, just as in the Caribbean banana exporting countries the EU is trying to protect, he said. Some 26 percent of producers owned less than five hectares and 85 percent of the trade was by Ecuadorean companies.
Employees in the sector were protected by strict labour laws and a minimum wage.

Despite large numbers of small producers Ecuador was a highly efficient producer - a tonne of Ecuadorean bananas cost $162 per tonne. "Some ACP countries are over $500. We have a clear competitive advantage," he said.

"We're not against aid to the Caribbean producers but we don't think it should be being done at our expense. The EU has to come up with imaginative ways to support efficient production in the Caribbean," Maldonado said.
Ecuador had been obliged to spend $40 million each year on export licences to export into the EU market, Maldonado said. --Christopher Lyddon, London newsroom +44 171 542 7928
